title: Judas didn’t wake up one morning and randomly decide to betray Jesus.
paragraphs: Judas didn’t wake up one morning and randomly decide to betray Jesus.
That’s the part people skip.

We reduce him to thirty pieces of silver… a kiss in the garden… a villain in the story. But the deeper lesson hiding inside Judas Iscariot is far more terrifying because it exposes something many believers secretly carry while still sitting in church, still lifting their hands, still walking near Jesus externally.
Hidden disappointment.
Not open rebellion.
Not atheism.
Not immediate hatred toward Christ.
Disappointment that stayed unspoken long enough to become darkness.
The tragedy of Judas was not merely betrayal.
It was proximity without surrender.
It was following Jesus while silently resenting the way Jesus refused to become the Messiah Judas wanted.
Most people never notice that Judas followed Christ for years while internally expecting a different kingdom.
A different outcome.
A different kind of power.
And disappointment hidden long enough can mutate into bitterness while the mouth still says “Rabbi.”
In John 12:4-6, Scripture reveals something chilling:

“But Judas Iscariot, one of His disciples (the one who was about to betray Him), said, ‘Why wasn’t this perfume sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?’ He didn’t say this because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief.”
The Greek word used for thief is:
κλέπτης (kleptēs)
Not merely someone tempted occasionally.
A stealer.
One who secretly takes.
Judas had already been hiding corruption before the betrayal ever manifested publicly.
That is how spiritual collapse often works.
The betrayal people see publicly usually began privately long before anyone noticed.
What makes Judas terrifying is that nobody at the table initially suspected him.
When Jesus said in Matthew 26:21:
“Truly I tell you, one of you will betray Me,”
the disciples began asking:
“Surely not I, Lord?”
None of them immediately pointed at Judas.
Why?
Because hidden disappointment often disguises itself extremely well inside religious behavior.
Judas looked close to Jesus externally.
But inwardly, something was dying.
The Hebrew understanding behind the idea of the “heart” matters deeply here.
In Scripture, the Hebrew word is:
לֵב (lev)
Not merely emotions.
The inner will.
The control center.
Mind, desires, intentions, affections.
Judas physically walked with Jesus while his lev slowly drifted somewhere else.
And many believers are doing the same thing right now.
Still attending church.
Still posting Bible verses.
Still saying “God is good.”
But secretly disappointed because Jesus did not answer the prayer the way they wanted.
Because the healing did not come.
Because the relationship died.
Because the ministry failed.
Because the suffering remained.
Because God did not perform according to their expectations.
And disappointment left unprocessed becomes spiritually dangerous.
Judas likely expected a conquering political Messiah.
Many Jews during that era anticipated a ruler who would overthrow Rome visibly and establish national dominance.
But Jesus kept talking about servanthood.
Dying.
Loving enemies.
Taking up crosses.
Losing your life to find it.
That was not the kingdom Judas envisioned.
And instead of bringing his confusion honestly before Christ… Judas concealed it.
That concealment became rot.
John 13:27 says:
“After Judas ate the piece of bread, Satan entered into him.”
The Greek phrase is deeply sobering:

εἰσῆλθεν εἰς ἐκεῖνον ὁ Σατανᾶς
(eisēlthen eis ekeinon ho Satanas)
“Entered into him.”
Notice something important.
Satan did not create the disappointment.
He exploited what Judas refused to surrender.
That changes everything.
Because many people think spiritual destruction begins with demons.
Often it begins with hidden wounds we refuse to bring honestly before Jesus.
Judas never openly wrestled.
Never openly confessed.

Never openly cried out:
“I don’t understand You anymore.”
Peter failed loudly.
Thomas doubted openly.
David wept publicly.
Jeremiah questioned God emotionally.
But Judas concealed everything behind the appearance of discipleship.
That is why hidden disappointment is so dangerous.
It can survive inside outward Christianity for years unnoticed.
One of the most heartbreaking moments comes in Matthew 26:50 when Jesus says to Judas:
“Friend, do what you came for.”
The Greek word used for “friend” here is:
ἑταῖρε (hetairos)
A companion.
An associate.
Jesus still addressed Judas with restrained mercy even in the moment of betrayal.
And this is where the article becomes painfully personal.
Some believers are not abandoning Jesus because they hate Him.
They are slowly drifting because He disappointed the version of Christianity they imagined.
They thought obedience would guarantee comfort.
They thought prayer would prevent suffering.
They thought faithfulness would remove warfare.
They thought serving God would make life easier.
Then reality collided with expectation.
And instead of grieving honestly before God… they buried the disappointment beneath religious routine.
But concealed disappointment eventually seeks escape.
For Judas, it became betrayal.
For others, it becomes cynicism.
Compromise.
Secret addictions.
Bitterness.
Deconstruction rooted not in intellectual questions but emotional wounds.
Coldness toward prayer.
Resentment toward God.
Performative Christianity without intimacy.
And the terrifying part is that people can remain around Jesus while internally walking away from Him.
That is the lesson Judas taught me.
Not merely betrayal.
Hidden disappointment left unhealed.
Psalm 62:8 says:
“Pour out your hearts before Him.”
The Hebrew phrase for “pour out” carries the imagery of spilling completely.
God never asked us to pretend before Him.
He already sees what is hidden.
The difference between Peter and Judas was not perfection.
Both failed Jesus.
Both broke under pressure.
But Peter returned weeping.
Judas returned despairing.
Peter ran toward grace.
Judas ran away from it.
And some people reading this are exhausted from pretending they are spiritually okay.
You still attend.
Still smile.
Still serve.
But secretly, there is disappointment toward God buried underneath your worship.
And if you never bring it into the light, the enemy will gladly build lies inside the silence.
Jesus is not afraid of your questions.
He is not intimidated by your confusion.
He is not shocked by your grief.
But hidden disappointment becomes deadly when honesty disappears.
The Gospel was never an invitation to perform emotional perfection.
It was an invitation to surrender truthfully.
Even now, Christ still calls wounded people closer.
Not farther.
The cross itself proves that God understood suffering better than we do.
Isaiah 53 says He was:
“A man of sorrows, acquainted with grief.”
The Hebrew phrase:

מַכְאֹבוֹת וִידוּעַ חֹלִי
(mak'ovot veyadua choli)
Means deep pains… familiar with sickness, suffering, grief.
Jesus understands disappointment from the inside.
That is why you do not have to hide it from Him.
And maybe that is the real warning inside Judas’ story.

Not simply:
“Don’t betray Jesus.”
But:
“Don’t silently drift from Him while pretending everything is fine.”
Bring the disappointment into the light before it becomes something darker.
Because concealed wounds eventually speak.
And when they do, they often speak destructively.
Some people do not need another motivational message.
They need permission to finally be honest before God.
Some betrayals begin long before the kiss ever happens.
